2027-03-21.alt: Hosanna Sunday (Oshana Njayar): the blessing of the palms, the procession and the Holy Qurbana. The Week of the Passion (Hasha Week) begins. Longer forms in the calendar: Genesis 49:1–12, 22–26; Matthew 20:29–21:22.
2027-03-21.verse: Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest heaven!
theo: Today the Church walks with Jesus into Jerusalem, and the Great Fast gives way to the Week of the Passion, which our tradition calls Hasha Week. Hosanna Sunday is one of the days Kerala Christians love most, and its rite is simple enough for every family to follow. First, the people gather before the Holy Qurbana, often outside the church or at a nearby cross, each holding a tender coconut leaf, the kuruthola. Second, the celebrant prays over the palms and blesses them, sprinkling them with holy water. Third, the Gospel of the Lord's entry into Jerusalem is proclaimed, so that we hear what we are about to do. Fourth, the procession moves toward the church and around it, with the cross going before, while everyone waves the palms and sings the Hosanna hymns, as the crowds did on the road from Bethphage. Fifth, the procession enters the church, and the Holy Qurbana continues with the readings of the day: the King we have welcomed with palms now comes to us on the altar. Afterwards the families take the blessed palms home and keep them in the prayer corner. On Pesaha a small cross folded from the blessed palm is pressed into the Pesaha appam; and many parishes keep the old palms to burn them for the ashes at the beginning of next year's Great Fast. So the palm of welcome, the bread of the Supper and the ashes of repentance are woven into one year of faith. Customs vary from eparchy to eparchy and parish to parish; follow the order your parish uses.

The first reading is the blessing of the dying Jacob over his sons. To Judah he says: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be on the neck of your enemies; your father's sons shall bow down before you.” And then a promise that Israel treasured for centuries: “The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him; and the obedience of the peoples is his.” Strangely, the next line speaks of a donkey: “Binding his foal to the vine and his donkey's colt to the choice vine, he washes his garments in wine and his robe in the blood of grapes.” The Fathers saw here the King from Judah who would come riding on a donkey's colt, and whose garments would be washed in the wine of his own blood. The reading also gives the blessing of Joseph, the son who suffered at the hands of his brothers and saved them: “Joseph is a fruitful bough, a fruitful bough by a spring; his branches run over the wall. The archers fiercely attacked him; they shot at him and pressed him hard. Yet his bow remained taut, and his arms were made agile by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob.” In the King from Judah and the rejected brother who saves his family, the Church has always seen one face: Jesus, the Son of David, who goes up to Jerusalem to be rejected and to save.

Zechariah's prophecy is the key to everything that happens on the road from Bethany: “Rejoice greatly, O daughter Zion! Shout aloud, O daughter Jerusalem! Lo, your king comes to you; triumphant and victorious is he, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.” Kings rode into cities on war horses. This King comes on a farmer's animal, and the prophet explains why: “He will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the war-horse from Jerusalem; and the battle bow shall be cut off, and he shall command peace to the nations.” He wins his kingdom not by killing but by dying, and he seals it “because of the blood of my covenant with you”. And he calls out to all who are trapped: “Return to your stronghold, O prisoners of hope.” In Kerala, where elephants and caparisons and loud processions mark our feasts, the Lord's chosen mount is a quiet rebuke and a great comfort. He does not come to frighten us; he comes humble, to set prisoners free.

Paul, writing to Gentile Christians in Rome, uses an image every Kerala farmer understands: grafting. The Church of Israel is a cultivated olive tree with a holy root. Some branches were broken off; the Gentiles, “a wild olive shoot”, have been grafted in “to share the rich root of the olive tree”. Paul's warning is sharp: “do not boast over the branches. If you do boast, remember that it is not you that support the root, but the root that supports you.” “So do not become proud, but stand in awe.” And he insists that God has not finished with his people: “God has the power to graft them in again.” This reading belongs on Hosanna Sunday. As we enter the Week of the Passion, the Church forbids us to blame the Jewish people as a whole for the death of Jesus; the Second Vatican Council teaches that the Jews remain most dear to God, whose gifts and call are irrevocable, and that his Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews of that time or of today. Christ died for the sins of all of us, and we are the branches who live from the root.

Then the Gospel. Jesus sends two disciples to bring a donkey and her colt, and Matthew tells us why: “This took place to fulfill what had been spoken through the prophet.” The crowds spread their cloaks on the road, cut branches from the trees, and shout: “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest heaven!” Hosanna is a Hebrew cry meaning “Save us, we pray”, taken from Psalm 118, the pilgrims' psalm. “When he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was in turmoil, asking, ‘Who is this?’” That question will echo through the whole week. Matthew goes straight on to the temple: Jesus drives out the sellers and buyers and overturns the tables, saying, “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’; but you are making it a den of robbers.” Then “the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he cured them”, and the children go on crying “Hosanna to the Son of David”. When the authorities object, Jesus quotes the psalm: “Out of the mouths of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise for yourself.” The King's first act in his city is to cleanse the house of prayer and to heal; and the purest praise comes from children. Today, as our children wave their palms, let us ask whether our own hearts, our homes and our parishes are houses of prayer, and whether the cry Hosanna on our lips today will still be there on Friday.
conn: The foal bound to the vine.
Jacob's blessing speaks of Judah binding his donkey's colt to the vine (Genesis 49:11); Jesus sends for a donkey tied with her colt and rides into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:2–7).
Zechariah's king comes humble, riding on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9), quoted at the entry (Matthew 21:5; John 12:14–15). Solomon too rode David's mule to be anointed king (1 Kings 1:33–39).

The crowd's cry comes from the pilgrims' psalm: “Save us, we beseech you, O Lord … Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord” (Psalm 118:25–26). The Church sings it in the Holy Qurbana before the Lord comes on the altar.

Cloaks were spread for Jehu when he was proclaimed king (2 Kings 9:13); palms and branches were carried when the temple was purified in the days of the Maccabees (2 Maccabees 10:7). John tells that the crowd took branches of palm trees (John 12:13).

Jesus joins Isaiah, “my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples” (Isaiah 56:7), and Jeremiah's warning against making it “a den of robbers” (Jeremiah 7:11). His own body is the new temple (John 2:19–21).

Paul's olive tree (Romans 11:17–24) is echoed by the Second Vatican Council: the Church draws sustenance from the root of that good olive tree onto which the Gentiles have been grafted (Nostra Aetate 4).
altar: The King who entered Jerusalem humble and riding on a donkey enters our church in the procession, and then comes truly on the altar in the Holy Qurbana; the Hosanna we sing before the anaphora greets the same Lord.
In the Holy Qurbana we receive the blood of the covenant of which Zechariah spoke, the blood that sets the prisoners of hope free.

Follow every day of the week

fathers: Let us go together to meet Christ on the Mount of Olives. Let us spread before his feet not garments or lifeless branches, but ourselves, clothed in his grace; and let us wave, not palm branches, but the palms of victory, crying with the children: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.

It was no promotion for the King of the ages to become the King of Israel; it was condescension. He did not come to exact tribute or to command armies, but to rule souls, to lead to heaven those who believe, hope and love.
magis: Jesus entered Jerusalem as the Messiah, Son of David, riding on a donkey; he is acclaimed by children and the poor, and the Church takes up their Hosanna in the Sanctus of the liturgy.
Jesus' entry into Jerusalem manifested the coming of the kingdom that the King-Messiah was going to accomplish by the Passover of his death and Resurrection; with it the Church begins Holy Week.
Jesus went up to the temple as the privileged place of encounter with God; he was angered that its outer court had become a place of commerce.
The historical complexity of Jesus' trial means that the Jews as a whole cannot be held responsible for his death; all sinners were the authors of his Passion.

The Church draws sustenance from the root of that good olive tree onto which the Gentiles have been grafted; the Jews remain most dear to God, and what happened in his Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today.
saints: The Week of the Passion (Hasha Week). 22–24 Mar: Monday to Wednesday of the Week of the Passion. 25 Mar: Pesaha, the Holy Qurbana of the Lord's Supper with the washing of feet (one Qurbana in each church); at home, the Pesaha appam and paal. The Annunciation (25 Mar) falls on Pesaha this year and is transferred as the Syro-Malabar Ordo directs (verify locally). 26 Mar: Passion Friday (Dukha Velli): the Way of the Cross, the veneration of the Cross, the bitter drink (kaippuneer). 27 Mar: Great Saturday. 28 Mar: Easter, the Resurrection (Uyirppu).
2027-03-21.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of David and King of peace, you came to Jerusalem humble and riding on a donkey, and the children cried Hosanna. Today we take up their cry: save us, we pray. Cleanse the temple of our hearts and make our homes houses of prayer. Keep us humble, grafted by grace into the olive tree of your people, and let our Hosanna not fall silent when the week grows dark, but follow you to the Cross and to the joy of your Resurrection. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

quick: The scepter of Judah and the humble King on a donkey: the prophecies meet on the road to Jerusalem.
Jesus cleanses the house of prayer, heals the blind and the lame, and accepts the praise of children.
We are branches grafted onto a holy root; no room for pride, only gratitude.

kidsaint: He was a Swiss farmer and the father of ten children, who died on 21 March 1487. Later in life, with his wife's agreement, he lived as a hermit and prayed for his country. When Switzerland was about to fall into civil war, the leaders asked his advice, and his words of peace kept the country together. Lesson: Jesus is the King of peace, and he wants us to be peacemakers too!
2027-03-21.special: Hosanna Sunday; the Week of the Passion begins.
term: A Hebrew cry meaning “Save us, we pray”, from Psalm 118. The crowds shouted it when Jesus entered Jerusalem; the Church sings it in the Holy Qurbana, and the Sunday before Easter takes its name from it.

family.explain: Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a little donkey. The people were so happy that they put their coats on the road and waved branches from the trees. They shouted: “Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!” Today we wave our palm leaves to welcome Jesus too. He is a King, but a gentle King who comes on a donkey, not on a war horse.
family.intention: We pray that our family may welcome Jesus into our home this week.
family.ask: Ask: “Where shall we keep our blessed palm, and how will we pray together each evening this week?”

illus: Every Hosanna Sunday a grandfather in a parish near Thodupuzha sat in the front pew with a bundle of blessed palms on his knees, folding small crosses for every child who came by. He had learnt it from his own grandmother. One year a boy asked him why he took so much trouble over leaves that would dry up in a week. He held up a cross and said: “On Sunday they shout Hosanna. On Friday they shout Crucify. I fold the leaf into a cross so that you will remember both, and stay with him all the way.”

pm.open: Lord Jesus, King of peace, you come to us humble and gentle. We welcome you with our Hosanna. Amen.
share: The scepter shall not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10). Do I let Jesus truly be the King of my life?
Lo, your king comes to you; triumphant and victorious is he, humble and riding on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9). Where do I need his gentleness rather than force?
It is not you that support the root, but the root that supports you (Romans 11:18). Where has pride crept into my faith?
My house shall be called a house of prayer (Matthew 21:13). What needs to be cleansed in the temple of my heart and my home?
interc: For the Church as she enters the Week of the Passion.
For the Pope, the bishops and all priests who will lead the rites of this holy week.
For peace among nations, through Christ the King of peace.
For the Jewish people, our elder brothers and sisters in faith.
For children, whose praise the Lord loves, and for our families as we follow him this week.
pm.close: Father, your Son entered Jerusalem humble and riding on a donkey, to give his life for us. Make us follow him faithfully this week, from the palms of Hosanna to the Cross and the empty tomb. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today we carried blessed palms and sang Hosanna, as the crowds did on the road into Jerusalem. The Great Fast now gives way to the Week of the Passion. The palms we take home will be folded into a cross for the Pesaha appam, and next year they will become the ashes of a new Great Fast.

Long ago Jacob blessed his son Judah: the scepter shall not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10). And he spoke of a donkey's colt bound to the vine. Today the Son of David from the tribe of Judah comes riding on that colt.

Zechariah tells us what kind of King he is: lo, your king comes to you; triumphant and victorious is he, humble and riding on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9). He does not come on a war horse. He comes to command peace to the nations and to set free the prisoners of hope by the blood of the covenant.

Paul warns us Gentile Christians not to boast: it is not you that support the root, but the root that supports you (Romans 11:18). This week we will hear the Passion. Let us never blame the Jewish people for the death of Jesus. He died for the sins of all of us.

The crowds cried: Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord! (Matthew 21:9). Hosanna means save us, we pray. Then Jesus cleansed the temple: my house shall be called a house of prayer (Matthew 21:13). He healed the blind and the lame, and the children went on singing.

The same crowd that sings Hosanna today will shout Crucify on Friday. Let our Hosanna last all week. Let our homes be houses of prayer, let us come to Pesaha, to Passion Friday and to the Easter Qurbana, and let us follow our humble King to the Cross and to the empty tomb. Amen.
kids: Children, today we waved palm leaves and sang Hosanna, just like the children in Jerusalem! Jesus loved hearing their praise.
Jesus came riding on a little donkey, not on a big war horse, because he is a gentle King of peace. Take your blessed palm home and keep it near the cross in your prayer corner.

opts.a: The blind, the lame and the children

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, when Jesus entered Jerusalem the whole city was in turmoil, asking: who is this? The crowds were saying: this is the prophet Jesus from Nazareth in Galilee (Matthew 21:10–11). They were right, but they did not yet know the whole truth. He is the Child of whom Isaiah said: he is named Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God (Isaiah 9:6).

Then Jesus went into the Temple. And the Gospel says: the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he cured them (Matthew 21:14). Long ago, when David captured Jerusalem, a saying arose that the blind and the lame shall not come into the house (2 Samuel 5:8). Now the Son of David opens the house of God to them. The King welcomes those who were kept outside.

And the children were crying out in the Temple: Hosanna to the Son of David. The chief priests and scribes became angry. Jesus answered with the Psalm: out of the mouths of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise for yourself (Matthew 21:16; Psalm 8:2). The learned were offended; the little ones understood.

Today our children carried the palms. Let us not think that Holy Week is only for adults. Let them come to Pesaha, to the Way of the Cross and to the Easter night. And let us bring the sick and the elderly too, those who find it hard to come. The Church is a house for the blind, the lame and the little ones.

So this week let us answer for ourselves the question of Jerusalem: who is this? Let us pray each evening with our children, and help someone weak to come to the Holy Qurbana. Then our Hosanna will be the Hosanna of the Temple, sung by simple hearts to a King who heals. Amen.

intro: The disciples were sent to untie a donkey and her colt, with only one explanation: the Lord needs them. Hosanna Sunday asks what we will give to the King.

sub: Two disciples sent to the village.
A simple animal given at once.
points.apply: Give the Lord one thing he asks of you this week without delay.

sub: Laying down what we have before the King.
points.apply: Lay down one comfort this week as a gift to Christ.

sub: A cry of praise and of need.

concl: The King asks for a donkey, for cloaks, for our cry.
Whatever we give him, he uses for his coming.
opts.resolve: This week I will give the Lord without delay whatever he asks of me, and pray often: Hosanna, save us.
homily: Dear friends, before the procession Jesus sent two disciples to a village and said: you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her; untie them and bring them to me. If anyone says anything to you, just say this: the Lord needs them (Matthew 21:2–3). The owner gave them at once.

Long ago Jacob had blessed Judah, speaking of a foal bound to the vine (Genesis 49:11). Now that promise comes true, and the King needs a simple animal. The Lord of all things does not need anything from us. And yet he chooses to need us. He asks for our time, our hands, our voice, so that he may come into the city of our world.

A very large crowd spread their cloaks on the road (Matthew 21:8). When Jehu was anointed king, the people hurriedly took their cloaks and spread them for him on the bare steps (2 Kings 9:13). A cloak was a poor person's covering and bed. To lay it on the road was to say: everything I have is yours. What cloak will we lay before the King this week? Our comfort, our sleep, our pride?

And the crowds cried: Hosanna to the Son of David! The word comes from the Psalm of the pilgrims: save us, we beseech you, O LORD (Psalm 118:25). It is praise and a cry for help together. All this week, in our need and in our joy, this can be our prayer: Hosanna, Lord, save us.

So let us untie whatever the Lord needs from us and give it without delay. Let us lay our cloaks before him. Let us follow him to Pesaha, to the Cross and to the empty tomb, crying Hosanna. And at the Holy Qurbana let us welcome him who comes in the name of the Lord. Amen.
